title: Director, Office of Workers' Compensation Programs v. Newport News Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Co.
lead: After an injured worker declined to appeal his partial-disability award, the federal program director sought review in her own name.

actors.name: Newport News Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Co.
Director of the Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs
actors.role: Labor Department administrator seeking judicial review

proceedings: Administrative law judge found partial disability; Benefits Review Board affirmed and approved a special-fund transfer.
Fourth Circuit rejected the Director’s standing on disability but allowed her fund challenge.
Supreme Court affirmed only the disability-appeal standing ruling.
limits: The statutory decision did not forbid Congress from authorizing agency appeals. Fund standing, proper respondent status, and the disability merits were reserved. Rulemaking discussion reflects the 1995 framework.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A back injury interrupts work
paragraphs: Jackie Harcum worked for Newport News Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Co. On October 24, 1984, metal grating fell on him while he worked in a steam barge’s bilge, injuring his lower back. Surgery removed a herniated disc. Newport News paid benefits until he returned to light duty in April 1987. That November he returned to his regular department under medical restrictions but could not perform essential tasks. The company terminated him in May 1988, and he found other work beginning in February 1989.

Harcum sought compensation for the interval between jobs. An administrative law judge found partial rather than total disability. The Benefits Review Board affirmed and held that employer payments could stop after 104 weeks, with a statutory special fund assuming responsibility.

sections.title: The administrator appeals when the worker does not
sections.cue: The Fourth Circuit separates two interests
paragraphs: The Director of the Labor Department’s Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs petitioned the Fourth Circuit to review both rulings. Harcum did not appeal. Although he did not oppose the Director’s petition, he expressly declined an invitation to intervene.

The Fourth Circuit raised standing itself. It held that the Director was not a person adversely affected or aggrieved by denial of full-disability benefits under § 21(c) of the Longshore and Harbor Workers’ Compensation Act. It separately allowed her challenge involving the special fund she administered. The Supreme Court reviewed only the disability-appeal ruling, leaving the fund issue unresolved.

The Director argued that an erroneous award frustrated her duties to secure proper compensation, administer the Act uniformly, and support effective informal settlements. The statutory process began with possible informal resolution by a district director, followed by an administrative law judge and the Board, but did not expressly make the program Director a party or authorize her appeal.

sections.title: Scalia finds no statutory appeal authority
sections.cue: A policy disagreement differs from injury as a market participant
paragraphs: Justice Scalia, writing for eight Justices, distinguished a government entity injured in the same capacity as a private participant, such as a shipper contesting an unlawful rate, from an administrator dissatisfied with a decision’s policy effects. Treating the latter interest as ordinary aggrievement would repeatedly put courts in intrabranch and intraagency disputes.

The phrase had an administrative-review history. The Administrative Procedure Act excluded agencies from its definition of person, while other statutes expressly authorized official appeals. The Occupational Safety and Health Act used general aggrieved-person language and separately empowered the Secretary to petition. The Black Lung Benefits Act expressly made the Secretary a party. Nothing extraordinary in this statutory scheme supplied the missing authorization.

Nor did the Act simply maximize employee recovery. It reflected an employer-worker compromise; the Director facilitated settlements and supplied information to both sides. Discretionary legal assistance to a requesting claimant did not create a duty to appeal independently after a claimant accepted an award. Cases involving federal guardianship of Indians or express civil-rights litigation authority showed Congress could authorize such litigation, not that it had done so here.

An erroneous award did not prevent processing claims, assisting participants, or enforcing final awards. Congress separated administration and adjudication in 1972. Under the administrative-law framework then applied, the Director retained rulemaking as a means to address disagreement with a Board rule of law. Predicted damage to settlement negotiations was speculative. Liberal construction could clarify an ambiguous statutory element, but could not add powers Congress had withheld merely to advance a remedial purpose.

sections.title: Ginsburg sees an omission Congress must correct
sections.cue: The worker’s disability classification is not reviewed
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg concurred only in the judgment. Before 1972, deputy commissioners adjudicated claims, defended their orders in district court, and could appeal adverse judgments. Moving adjudication to administrative law judges and review to the Board removed that route without explicit discussion of administrator appeals. Later Black Lung legislation authorized participation and appeared to contemplate similar operation of the two programs; earlier Supreme Court cases had generally overlooked the changed standing problem.

Ginsburg also identified four other federal compensation systems using Longshore procedures. The same administrators could confront identical issues while possessing appeal authority only under Black Lung. She regarded that disparity as apparent oversight, but correction required congressional judgment beyond fixing a scrivener’s error.

On March 21, 1995, the Court unanimously affirmed the Fourth Circuit’s disability-appeal standing ruling. It did not determine Harcum’s disability, resolve special-fund standing, or decide whether the Director could be a respondent in someone else’s appeal. Power to initiate review was the distinct statutory question decided.
